q: The outer layers of each grain are milled off before brewing mainly to get rid of what?
opts: Protein and fat, which throw coarse off-flavours
Starch, which the yeast cannot ferment
Colour compounds that would tint the sake
exp: Protein, fat and minerals concentrate near the surface and produce heavy, savoury notes. Milling is slow work and can take two or three days for a competition sake.

q: Which organism is cultivated on steamed rice to break the starch down into fermentable sugar?
exp: Aspergillus oryzae releases enzymes that cleave starch into glucose. Yeast then eats that glucose, so the two organisms have entirely separate jobs.

q: Saccharification and alcoholic fermentation run at the same time in the same tank. What is that arrangement called?
exp: Sugar is released only as fast as the yeast consumes it, so the mash never becomes syrupy. It is why sake reaches close to 20 percent alcohol without fortification.

q: Where is the mould propagated during the two days or so that it takes to make koji?
opts: In the pressing shed alongside the finished mash
In the koji muro, a warm and humid dedicated room
exp: The muro is held warm and damp and the rice is turned by hand through the night. It is the stage brewers describe as the one that decides the sake.

q: Barley malt supplies its own enzymes to a beer mash. What does that job in a sake mash?
exp: Malting germinates the barley and wakes its enzymes. Rice has no equivalent trick, so the enzymes have to be supplied from outside by the mould.

q: After the rice has been washed and soaked, how is it prepared for the mould and the mash?
opts: It is boiled in water until soft
It is steamed rather than boiled
It is roasted dry over a flame
It is milled for a second time
exp: Steaming firms the outside of the grain while softening the inside, which is exactly what the mould needs. Boiled rice turns to paste and is useless for brewing.

q: Which stage supplies the dense, healthy yeast population that goes on to drive the main mash?
exp: The shubo, also called the moto, concentrates yeast in a small, acidic volume before it is scaled up. Building it takes anywhere from two weeks to a month depending on the method.

q: A brewery adds lactic acid directly to the starter to keep spoilage organisms out while the yeast builds. Which method is that?
exp: Sokujo is the modern default and takes about two weeks. Kimoto and yamahai instead wait for ambient lactic bacteria to acidify the starter, which takes far longer.

q: Why is the main mash built up in three staged additions spread across four days?
opts: To make the mash easier to press
To keep the yeast in the majority
To lower the final alcohol content
exp: Adding all the rice and water at once would dilute the yeast and let spoilage organisms take hold, so each addition keeps the population dense enough to stay dominant as the volume grows. A rest day between the first and second additions lets the yeast catch up.

q: Once fermentation finishes the mash is pressed. What is the solid residue left behind?
exp: The pressed lees, sold as sake kasu, are a valued ingredient in their own right, used for pickling vegetables and fish and for the winter soup kasujiru. Nothing about them is waste.

q: A bottle carries no grade beyond the brewery name and accounts for the bulk of what Japan drinks. What is that category?
exp: Ordinary sake sits outside the eight special designations and faces looser rules on milling and additions. Premium grades are the minority of national output.

q: Which word on a label guarantees that nothing but rice, water, koji and yeast went in?
exp: Junmai means pure rice. It says nothing by itself about how far the rice was milled, so junmai can be anything from workmanlike to superb.

q: A small, measured quantity of distilled alcohol has been stirred into the mash before pressing. Which designation covers that?
exp: The addition is capped at 10 percent of the weight of the polished rice. It lifts aroma out of the mash and lightens the body rather than stretching the volume.

q: No more than what proportion of each grain may remain for a sake to be labelled ginjo?
exp: Ginjo also demands careful, cool, slow brewing on top of the milling figure. Honjozo needs 70 percent or less, and daiginjo 50 percent or less.

q: Two bottles show milling figures of 50 percent and 60 percent. What is the highest grade each figure unlocks?
exp: Fifty percent or less opens the door to daiginjo, sixty percent or less to ginjo. Add junmai to either name and the sake also has no added alcohol.

q: The prefix tokubetsu sits in front of junmai or honjozo on a label. What is the brewery claiming?
opts: That the sake was never pasteurised
Extra milling or a special method
That the sake was aged for ten years
exp: Tokubetsu means special, and the brewery has to say what the special element is. Usually it is milling to 60 percent or the use of a single prized rice.
